title: Europe’s Dangerous Hesitation on Its Own Air Defense
gist: Interceptor arithmetic is unwinnable — the U.S. makes a little over 600 PAC-3s a year while Ukraine alone burns 150–180 in a month of intensive attack — so NATO’s only viable counter to massed ballistic missiles is “shooting the archer”: deep strikes on launchers and missile plants inside Russia, which NATO doctrine already mandates but which European political leaders privately will not authorize.

insights.claim: The United States produces a little more than 600 PAC-3 interceptors annually with a goal of tripling that, while Ukraine alone can burn through 150 to 180 in a single month of intensive Russian attacks.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: The production-to-consumption ratio is the hard number behind every interceptor procurement decision — solid rocket motor and seeker capacity is the sector bottleneck to watch.
insights.locator: The United States produces a little more than 600 PAC-3

insights.claim: Trump has backed away from hints that he might license Ukraine to build Patriot interceptors, and Washington has also declined Kyiv’s request for 300 interceptors.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: U.S. interceptor policy has tightened, not loosened — European buyers face a longer queue and stronger incentive to fund non-U.S. alternatives.

insights.claim: Even granting a license would not help Ukraine near-term because building new production facilities takes years and the Trump administration appears unwilling to share sensitive interceptor technology including seekers, solid rocket motors, and guidance software.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: Technology-transfer refusal is the durable constraint; licensing headlines should not be traded as capacity additions.
insights.locator: It would take years to build new production facilities

insights.claim: For the foreseeable future Ukraine’s anti-ballistic missile defense will still depend on drawdowns from allied stockpiles and stopgap systems, complemented by Ukrainian and European projects to build Patriot alternatives.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: Continued allied stockpile drawdowns mean European and U.S. inventories keep shrinking — a structural tailwind for interceptor and air-defense primes.

insights.claim: NATO members have strangely still not fast-tracked large-scale interceptor production in year five of Russia’s war, and interceptor numbers are unlikely to catch up with the ballistic missile potential of Russia and other adversaries any time soon.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: The rearmament narrative overstates delivered capacity; the gap between defense budgets announced and interceptors produced is where the real signal is.
insights.locator: Ukraine’s air defense problem should trigger a serious debate

insights.claim: The alternative to intercepting incoming missiles is “shooting the archer” — destroying the adversary’s launchers deep in the rear and, above all, its ballistic missile production facilities — which requires different weaponry and carries escalation risk.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: This doctrine shift favors long-range strike weapons, ISR, and cruise missile producers over pure interceptor programs in future procurement.

insights.claim: Ukraine has used four FP-5 Flamingo missiles to hit the Titan-Barrikady plant in Volgograd, roughly 400 km from the Ukrainian border, and the VNIIR-Progress plant in Cheboksary, both of which produce components for Russian missile types.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: Ukraine has operationalized deep strike against missile-component plants at 400 km-plus range — proof of concept that European deep-strike programs will cite.

insights.claim: Ukraine’s long-range drone and missile campaign against oil refineries, fuel depots, supply ships, port infrastructure, and defense-industrial plants is aimed at systematically degrading Russia’s ability to wage war and reduce missiles launched at Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: Russian refinery and port capacity remains a live target set — a recurring supply-side risk for crude products and Black Sea logistics.

insights.claim: U.S. and Israeli offensive operations against Iranian launchers and command sites likely did more to relieve pressure on Israel’s defenses than its interceptor stockpile, which media reports say is running dangerously low.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: The Iran campaign is the empirical case for offense-over-defense economics in missile warfare — expect it to reshape allied air-defense budgets.
insights.locator: The other example of a shoot-the-archer approach

insights.claim: Interceptor shortages in Israel and elsewhere act as a real constraint on the United States’ ability to continue a high-intensity war against Iran.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: Magazine depth, not political will, may be what caps the duration of the Iran conflict — a underappreciated de-escalation mechanism.

insights.claim: NATO’s new multi-domain operations doctrine already calls for deep strikes against air defenses, key infrastructure nodes, and critical industrial production in a conventional war with Russia, yet German civilian policymakers view exactly that approach as very risky and escalatory.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: NATO’s declared warfighting concept is not politically underwritten — deterrence credibility is weaker than force structure implies.
insights.locator: Based on conversations that I recently had with German civilian policymakers

insights.claim: There is a gap between what NATO military commanders assume they would be permitted to do based on doctrine and what political leaders in each individual capital would actually authorize.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: Assess European deterrence at the level of national political authorization, not alliance doctrine — that is where it fails.
insights.locator: In my conversations with NATO military officials

insights.claim: Germany’s planned procurement of U.S. Tomahawk long-range cruise missiles would have little deterrent value if Russia is convinced that Berlin, fearing escalation, would never use them.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: Capability purchases without declared employment doctrine buy hardware, not deterrence — a caution on reading European defense orders as strategic change.
insights.locator: The question of defense using deep strikes has become more timely

insights.claim: Germany still refuses to transfer Taurus cruise missiles to Ukraine and SpaceX does not allow Ukraine to use Starlink over Russian territory, with Zelensky reportedly asking Trump to help change that policy.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: A private company’s service geofence is now a binding constraint on state military operations — a governance risk for any defense architecture dependent on commercial space.

insights.claim: Russia would almost certainly attempt nuclear blackmail in a war and could view deep strikes as threatening its nuclear arsenal, anti-missile defense, and early warning system, amplifying the fear that paralyzes European decision-making.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: Nuclear entanglement is the deliberate lever Moscow uses to freeze European responses — expect it in every future crisis scenario.

insights.claim: Russia would likely entangle nuclear and conventional military capabilities so that any strike carries the risk of hitting something nuclear, mirroring China’s approach of mixing nuclear and nonnuclear systems.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: Deliberate target ambiguity is a reusable model both Moscow and Beijing use to raise the political cost of any Western strike — assume it in Taiwan scenarios too.

insights.claim: Fear of nuclear escalation repeatedly delayed weapons supplies to Kyiv from HIMARS to ATACMS and their use inside Russia, but most delays were eventually overcome and Moscow’s red lines proved more elastic than advertised.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: The empirical record argues escalation risk has been systematically overpriced — a reason to expect further loosening of Western strike constraints.
insights.quote: Most delays were eventually overcome, and Moscow’s red lines proved to be more elastic than advertised—an important data point for the escalation debate.

insights.claim: Drawn-out public Western debates about each new weapon type forewarned Russia and reduced the weapons’ impact by the time they finally arrived in Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: Public deliberation destroys the operational value of transferred systems — a reason future transfers will be quieter and harder to track.

insights.claim: Russia is pursuing a systems warfare approach aimed at degrading NATO’s defense industrial base, rear logistics, and critical infrastructure, meaning future great-power war will be characterized by deep precision strikes.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: European defense plants, logistics hubs, and grid infrastructure are explicit wartime targets — a hardening and insurance cost that is not yet in most models.

insights.claim: A NATO that credibly signals it will shoot the archer as well as defend against incoming missiles would strengthen deterrence, while visibly hesitant political leaders invite Moscow to believe saturation attacks on European cities could be sustained with impunity.
insights.speaker: Franz-Stefan Gady
insights.so_what: Watch for explicit European statements on deep-strike willingness — that declaratory shift, more than budget numbers, would mark a real change in the deterrence balance.
insights.quote: Conversely, political leaders who visibly hesitate invite Moscow to believe that saturation attacks on European cities could be sustained with impunity.
